planting.note: Set out young container plants in spring on lean, fast-draining, slightly acidic soil in full sun; broom seedlings form a deep taproot early and resent being moved, so pick the permanent site before planting.

directions: Set out young container-grown plants in spring on lean, fast-draining soil in full sun, choosing the final location carefully since the deep taproot makes later transplanting difficult. Common broom forms a dense, upright mass of slender, nearly leafless green stems that stay photosynthetically active year-round, and in mid to late spring it is smothered in bright yellow (sometimes red- or bicolor-flushed) pea-shaped flowers borne singly along the previous year's wood. It thrives in poor, sandy, or rocky soils of low fertility and actually performs worse in rich garden beds, since as a legume it fixes its own nitrogen. Shear lightly immediately after flowering to keep plants compact, because old bare wood rarely resprouts if cut back hard; note that this species has become seriously invasive along the US and Canadian Pacific coast and in parts of Australia and New Zealand, so gardeners there should seek sterile or regionally non-invasive cultivars instead of the wild-type species.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown plants in spring on lean, well-drained soil in full sun; propagate by cuttings rather than seed to keep the bicolor flower color true.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown plants in spring on lean, well-drained soil in full sun. 'Andreanus' is a long-cultivated sport of common broom discovered in France in the 1880s, prized for its strikingly bicolor flowers: each pea-shaped bloom has clear yellow upper petals (standard) and a maroon-crimson lower keel, giving the whole shrub a two-toned glow when it flowers heavily in late spring. Like the species, it keeps its fine green stems attractive through the rest of the year and tolerates poor, rocky, infertile soil far better than rich, heavily watered beds. Because seedlings revert toward plain yellow, propagate only from cuttings to preserve the bicolor trait, and shear lightly right after bloom rather than cutting into old bare wood.

common_name: Sunningdale Silver Pampas Grass (RHS Award-Winning Silver-Plumed Pampas Grass)

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in spring after the last frost in a permanent, full-sun site with excellent drainage; this selection is slower to establish than it is to outgrow its space, so allow a full-size footprint from the start.

directions: Plant container-grown divisions in spring after the last frost in a permanent, full-sun site with sharply drained soil; established clumps need little supplemental water. 'Sunningdale Silver' is one of the oldest and most widely grown named pampas grass selections, valued for producing exceptionally tall, dense, pure-silvery-white plumes held well above the arching blue-green foliage from late summer into winter, with a reputation for flowering more reliably and abundantly than many unnamed seedling plants sold as straight species. The sharp-edged leaves demand leather gloves for any handling, grooming, or division, which is best done with a sharp spade in early spring as new growth starts. Remove old flower stalks and tired foliage in late winter to keep the clump tidy before new growth resumes, and avoid planting it where it could seed into wild areas, since pampas grass is considered invasive in parts of coastal California and the Gulf Coast.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants after all frost danger in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; in borderline climates it can also be grown in a large container and trained against a warm wall.

directions: Set out container-grown plants after frost danger has passed, in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Native to southern Africa, lavender starflower is a sprawling, semi-deciduous shrub with glossy, scalloped leaves and an extended bloom season of lavender-pink, star-shaped, five-petaled flowers with a distinctive ring of darker stamens at the center, followed by unusual four-lobed, berry-like brown fruit that gives rise to the 'four-corner' common name. It can be grown as a loose informal hedge, trained on a trellis as a flowering vine, or kept pruned into a more compact rounded shrub, and it tolerates heat, wind, and poor soil once established. Prune after flowering to control size and encourage denser branching, and protect from hard frost, since it is reliably hardy only in essentially frost-free or very mild winter climates.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; variegation is best preserved by propagating from cuttings rather than seed.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown plants in spring in average, well-drained soil, siting in full sun for the strongest variegation or light afternoon shade in the hottest climates. This sport of common myrtle carries small, aromatic, glossy green leaves edged in creamy white, giving the whole shrub a brighter, more luminous presence than the plain green species while retaining the same fragrant summer flush of small white, five-petaled, fluffy-stamened flowers and the resulting blue-black berries. It responds well to shearing and is traditionally used for low formal hedging, topiary, and container specimens in courtyards, since it holds a clipped shape readily and the variegated foliage is attractive year-round. Protect from hard freezes and prolonged waterlogging, both of which it tolerates poorly compared with the plain species.

common_name: Broadway Mint Griselinia (Cream-Splashed New Zealand Broadleaf)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this coastal species tolerates salt spray and wind exceptionally well, making it a reliable seaside hedging choice.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown plants in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. 'Broadway Mint' is a variegated New Zealand broadleaf selection whose thick, glossy, apple-green leaves are splashed and mottled with creamy mint and pale yellow, brightening what is otherwise a plain dark-green hedging species while keeping the same dense, wind- and salt-tolerant habit. It is most often grown as a clipped hedge, screen, or specimen shrub in coastal gardens, where its leathery leaves shrug off salt spray and strong onshore winds far better than most variegated shrubs. Trim in mid to late summer to maintain a tidy shape, and avoid heavy, waterlogged soils; in colder inland climates it benefits from a sheltered site out of the harshest winter wind.
